To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a theoretical basis for the quantification of drug distribution in the ear can be established; 2) cochlear fluid space dimensions can be derived from three-dimensional MRIs; 3) the published time course of Gentamicin in vestibule perilymph can be closely approximated by adjustment of parameters defining the round window membrane permeabilty, clearance and interscala exchange; and 4) the effects of different round-window delivery methods can be calculated.

the time course and spatial distribution of gentamicin after round window application can be predicted with a computer model that incorporates the dimensions of the chichnilla inner ear and the known pharmacokinetic properties of gentamicin.

the time course of genta-micin in vestibular fluid after round window application was simulated by a pharmacokinetic model that considered diffusion, clearance, intercompartmental ex-change, and the dimensions of the ear.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a theoretical basis for the quantitative assessment of local delivery of antibiotics to the inner ear.
establishing a theoretical basis for understanding drug distribution in the cochlea.
the analysis of gentamicin kinetics in fluids of the inner ear with round window administration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the model developed here can be used to estimate the concentration of gentamicin delivered to the perilymph of the inner ear following application through the round window membrane, and that this concentration is dependent on the rate of application and duration of application of the drug.
this work provides a theoretical basis for understanding the kinetics of drugs applied to the round window and for quantifying drug levels and distribution in the inner ears with local applications.
the model provides a useful tool to predict the concentration-time profile of a drug delivered to the inner ear by round window administration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a mathematical model that can be used to predict the distribution of a drug in the inner ear following local application and to compare different methods of delivery.
the simulator can be used to calculate drug distribution in the ear for a given delivery method and to compare delivery methods for a given drug.
a theoretical basis for the analysis of local delivery to the inner ears has been established.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the time course of gentamycin in the inner ear can be closely simulated with a model based on pharmacokinetic principles, and this can be used to predict drug levels in different regions of the inner ear.
the time the applied gentamicin remains in the middle ear is a key factor in determining the amount of drug entering the inner ear and the resulting spatial distribution.
it is possible to develop a theoretical basis for predicting the time course of drug concentration in inner ear fluids with local drug delivery.
